name: Linux SCTP root
tile_line: Needs code on the box. No stable kernel fix yet.
summary: A bug in the Linux kernel's SCTP code lets any local user, including one inside a container, free the same kernel memory twice and take over the machine. Xint chained it with nginx2root to get root on the host and escape a Docker container. The fix reached the main kernel tree on 19 Nov, but no stable kernel has it yet and almost no distro ships it, so blocking the sctp module is the stopgap.

affected.label: Kernel 4.15 or later
affected.text: The bug arrived in 4.15 (Jan 2018). The fix was merged into the main kernel tree on 19 Nov, after 7.4-rc3. The newest stable kernels (7.3.5, 6.18.64, 6.12.118, released 17 Nov) don't have it, and on 22 Nov it wasn't queued for the next ones either; the only distro kernels we found carrying it are Gentoo's kernel sources and a Fedora Rawhide test build. Xint hasn't named the fix, but the commit credits Xint's tool and matches its description.

affected.label: Untrusted code can run on it
affected.text: The attacker must already run code on the machine, as any user or inside a container. Xint got there through nginx2root. The bug needs no special rights. Containers don't stop it: they share the host kernel, Docker's default seccomp profile doesn't block SCTP sockets, and Kubernetes pods run without seccomp unless you turn it on.

affected.label: SCTP can load
affected.text: The kernel loads the sctp module the first time any program opens an SCTP socket, unless it's blocked. Many distros ship it. Red Hat says it isn't loaded by default on RHEL: it's in kernel-modules-extra, which blacklists it on install. If `lsmod` prints nothing, it can still load on demand; `modprobe -c | grep sctp` shows any block.

do.label: Block SCTP if you don't use it
do.text: Put this line in a file under /etc/modprobe.d/ (Ubuntu uses disable-sctp.conf); on Debian and Ubuntu, then run `sudo update-initramfs -u`. It doesn't unload a module that's already loaded (reboot, or `sudo rmmod sctp` if nothing uses it) and doesn't help if SCTP is built into the kernel. It breaks telecom signalling and some Kubernetes network plugins. Red Hat's version is `install sctp /bin/true` plus `blacklist sctp`.

do.label: Update the kernel and reboot
do.text: Install your distro's kernel with the fix ("sctp: do not free a new asoc peeled off while sendmsg slept") once it ships, then reboot. No stable release has it as of 22 Nov, and it isn't queued for the next stable releases yet; Debian unstable's 7.3.5-1 doesn't have it either.

do.label: Patch the way in
do.text: Xint's chain starts with nginx2root, so upgrade nginx too. Any other way to run code on the host or in a container works just as well.

slack: Linux SCTP local root / container escape (no CVE yet): double free in the kernel's SCTP send path, in kernels since 4.15 (2018), reachable by any unprivileged local user, including inside a container. Xint chained it with nginx2root to get host root and escape Docker. Fix merged into mainline on 19 Nov (7.4-rc4); no stable kernel has it yet (22 Nov). Docker's default seccomp doesn't block SCTP. No public exploit, no attacks reported. Stopgap: `install sctp /bin/false` in /etc/modprobe.d/ (doesn't unload a loaded module, useless if SCTP is built in); check with `lsmod | grep sctp`.
